questions.q: What is the primary advantage of pybind11 over writing a CPython C API extension by hand?
options: pybind11 removes the need to compile any C++ code at all
pybind11 reads ordinary C++ declarations and generates the binding glue automatically
pybind11 makes C++ run faster than a native Python extension
pybind11 replaces the need for a C++ compiler entirely
questions.explain: pybind11 is a header-only library that generates the CPython glue code from your existing C++ function and class declarations, avoiding hand-written reference counting and boilerplate. It still compiles to a native extension.

questions.q: In `PYBIND11_MODULE(quantlib_cpp, m) { ... }`, what does the second argument, `m`, represent?
options: The name Python will use in an `import` statement
A `py::module_` object that functions and classes are attached to inside the block
The compiled filename of the shared library
A required but unused placeholder argument
questions.explain: The first argument (`quantlib_cpp`) is the importable module name; the second (`m`) is the `py::module_` object you call `.def(...)` and build `py::class_<...>(m, ...)` on inside the macro body.

questions.q: Which line correctly binds a free function `blackScholesCall` with a named keyword argument `spot`?
options: m.def("black_scholes_call", &blackScholesCall, py::arg("spot"));
m.bind("black_scholes_call", blackScholesCall, "spot");
m.function("black_scholes_call")(blackScholesCall)("spot");
py::def("black_scholes_call", &blackScholesCall, arg("spot"));
questions.explain: `m.def(name, &function, py::arg("paramName"), ...)` is the correct pybind11 pattern: `m.def` binds the function, and `py::arg` names each parameter so Python can call it with keywords.

options: Declares the Python-visible type `Bond` and binds a constructor taking a double, double, and int
Creates a Python dictionary named `Bond` with three default keys
Binds a static method named `init` that takes no arguments
Registers `Bond` as a module-level function rather than a class
questions.explain: `py::class_<Bond>(m, "Bond")` registers the C++ class `Bond` under the Python name `"Bond"`, and `.def(py::init<double, double, int>())` binds a constructor matching that parameter list.

questions.q: Why does automatic type conversion work seamlessly for a `double` or `int` argument but become a real design problem once a binding needs to accept a NumPy array?
options: NumPy arrays cannot be passed to any compiled language under any circumstances
A `double` and `int` are simple value types pybind11 converts by default; an array involves a buffer, shape, and memory-ownership questions pybind11 does not resolve automatically without extra work
pybind11 does not support NumPy at all, regardless of effort
Python ints and doubles are actually C++ objects already, so no conversion ever happens
questions.explain: Scalar types convert automatically because they are simple values. Arrays carry a buffer, shape/stride information, and ownership semantics, which require the dedicated NumPy support covered in the next lesson (`py::array_t` and the buffer protocol).
